property_summary: Only the originally recorded owner address can successfully cause the contract to transfer out its entire balance via withdrawAll (i.e., withdrawAll reverts for callers != owner).
Calling withdrawAll reverts for any caller that is not the contract's owner (msg.sender != owner).
Only direct calls where msg.sender equals the contract owner can successfully call withdrawAll (calls from intermediary contracts must revert).
withdrawAll always reverts when invoked by an address different from the contract owner (i.e., msg.sender != owner).
Calls to withdrawAll revert whenever the caller (msg.sender) is a contract (i.e., not an EOA), because onlyOwner compares msg.sender to owner.

For every caller and target, a call to sendMoney(target, value) made by the contract owner (msg.sender == owner) must not change the contract balance after the call (i.e., owner can only send funds out and balance decreases predictably); the mutant that uses tx.origin in onlyOwner can allow a non-owner EOA to trigger owner-only functions via an intermediate contract, causing differing post-call balances when sendMoney is invoked through an adversarial contract.

For any caller and any target/value, calls to sendMoney(target,value) initiated by the contract owner always leave the contract's owner-controlled withdrawal ability intact (owner can still withdraw the contract balance afterwards); the mutant that compares tx.origin instead of msg.sender can allow an intermediate contract to satisfy onlyOwner for sendMoney while preventing the real owner (msg.sender) from later withdrawing, breaking this invariant for some inputs (an adversarial intermediary and value).

For every caller and target, if the contract owner (msg.sender == owner) calls sendMoney(target, value) successfully, then afterwards the owner can still withdraw the contract's balance; the mutant (which checks tx.origin) can allow an intermediate contract to call sendMoney while tx.origin matches owner but msg.sender is the intermediary, causing the owner to be unable to withdraw afterwards for some adversarial intermediary and value.

For every target contract address and value, if the genuine owner (msg.sender == owner) directly calls sendMoney(target, value) from the owner EOA, then afterwards the owner can still withdraw the contract's remaining balance; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead of msg.sender can be tricked by an intermediate adversarial contract so that after sendMoney the owner can no longer withdraw for some target/value.

Reference: onlyOwner requires msg.sender==owner, so if an EOA other than owner calls sendMoney (i.e., msg.sender != owner) the call must revert; Mutant: uses tx.origin==owner so an intermediate contract can originate from owner and allow a non-owner msg.sender (the intermediary) to pass, making sendMoney succeed for non-owner msg.sender and thus differing behavior.

For any external callee that may revert on receiving funds, the reference contract's withdrawAll forwards the balance via its internal withdraw method using .call (so the withdrawAll call will revert if the transfer to msg.sender fails), whereas the mutant that uses direct transfer to msg.sender can trigger different behaviour when the recipient is a contract whose fallback/receive reverts — thus the reference always reverts/behaves consistently for such adversarial recipients while the mutant can succeed or behave differently for some inputs.

For any recipient contract address and any starting contract balance, calling withdrawAll() from the owner always results in the contract having zero balance afterward in the reference (because it calls withdraw(address(this).balance) which uses a low-level call to the recipient), but the mutant that replaces that with payable(msg.sender).transfer(address(this).balance) can leave balance non-zero when the recipient reverts on receiving funds; thus reference always reduces address(c).balance to 0 while mutant can fail to do so for some recipient.

For any recipient contract that may revert when receiving Ether, the reference C's withdrawAll (which calls withdraw(address(this).balance) -> withdraw uses low-level call and bubbles failure) always results in address(c).balance == 0 after a successful withdrawAll call by owner, while the mutant that directly uses payable(msg.sender).transfer(...) can leave address(c).balance non-zero for some adversarial recipient that reverts on receive; we assert that after invoking withdrawAll as owner the contract balance is zero (reference satisfies for all admissible inputs, mutant is broken for some).

For any owner caller and any recipient contract, if the owner calls withdrawAll() while the contract holds some Ether, the reference C always results in the contract balance becoming zero afterwards; the mutant that replaces the internal low-level call path with a direct transfer to msg.sender can leave the contract balance non-zero for some adversarial recipient that reverts on receive.

For any caller that is the owner and any initial contract balance, calling withdrawAll() always results in the caller (owner) receiving the full balance and thus address(c).balance == 0 afterwards in the reference; the mutant that replaces the internal call path with a direct transfer can fail to send funds to certain recipient contracts (e.g., contracts whose receive/fallback revert when called in the transfer context), leaving address(c).balance > 0 for some fuzzed amounts and adversarial recipient, which breaks the rule.

For any caller, calling withdrawAll must only succeed when the caller is the contract owner (so after a withdrawAll attempt by any non-owner, the contract balance remains unchanged); the mutant removing onlyOwner allows a non-owner to successfully drain the contract, breaking this rule.

For any caller and any initial balance, only the owner can successfully withdraw the contract's entire balance via withdrawAll (so non-owners cannot reduce address(c).balance); the mutant removing onlyOwner allows a non-owner to drain balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For all callers and initial balances, only the contract owner can successfully reduce address(c).balance by calling withdrawAll; the mutant removing onlyOwner allows some non-owner caller to succeed and thus reduce the balance.

For every non-owner caller and any initial contract balance funded via fallback, calling withdrawAll must NOT decrease address(c).balance (only the owner can withdraw everything); the mutant removing onlyOwner allows a non-owner caller to drain the contract and thus decrease address(c).balance for some inputs.

For every caller address and any initial contract balance funded via fallback by the owner, only the owner can successfully withdraw the entire contract balance via withdrawAll (so a non-owner call to withdrawAll must not succeed in reducing address(c).balance) — the mutant removes the onlyOwner guard allowing some non-owner to drain the contract, violating this rule.

For any deposit amount sent to the contract by the owner via fallback, calling withdrawAll returns the full contract balance to the owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) breaks this by leaving funds in the contract for some deposit amounts.

For any owner-deposited positive balance, calling withdrawAll by the owner reduces address(c).balance to 0 (reference calls withdraw(balance)); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a positive balance, violating this rule for some fuzzed deposit amount.

If the owner deposits a positive amount into the contract (via fallback), then after the owner calls withdrawAll the contract balance becomes 0 in the reference but the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a positive balance; we fuzz the deposit amount and the depositor address and assert that after deposit+withdrawAll the contract balance is zero (the mutant will fail for some deposits).

For any non-owner address that sends a positive amount to the contract, if the owner subsequently calls withdrawAll, the contract's balance becomes 0 (reference calls withdraw(balance)); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave that balance > 0 for some fuzzed deposit amounts and depositor addresses.

For any positive deposit amount sent into C by any depositor, when the owner calls withdrawAll the contract balance becomes 0 (reference calls withdraw with full balance); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a positive balance and thus violates this rule for some deposit amounts.
Only the owner can successfully withdraw funds from the contract (non-owners' withdraw attempts must fail or not transfer balance).
Withdraw calls revert for callers that are not the contract owner (i.e., non-owner withdraw attempts must fail).
If this test contract is not the owner of C, calling c.withdraw(0) must revert (i.e., reverted == true).
If this test contract is not the owner of C, calling c.withdraw(0) must revert (i.e., reverted == true).

sendMoney never reverts when called by owner with value <= contract balance (i.e., a successful send must not revert), so calling sendMoney as owner with an affordable amount should not cause revert and should decrease target's balance by that amount.

property_summary: When the owner calls sendMoney with value 0, the original contract's sendMoney never reverts (reverted == false) while the mutant using transfer may revert, so assert that reverted is false for value == 0 when caller is owner.

For any target address and payment amount where the target's receive/fallback reverts, the reference contract's sendMoney (which uses low-level call and checks its returned bool) will not revert the whole call and will report success (no revert) while the mutant using transfer will revert; thus the reference never causes the whole sendMoney call to revert for a reverting callee, but the mutant sometimes does.

For any target address and amount, C.sendMoney never reverts when the callee's fallback/receive reverts (because it uses a low-level call and checks the boolean), but the mutant using transfer will revert for such failing callees; therefore the reference always returns ok==true (no revert) while the mutant can make the call revert (ok==false).

For any target address and amount, C.sendMoney using a low-level call never reverts even if the callee's fallback/receive reverts (the call returns/handles failure), whereas the mutant using transfer will revert when the callee reverts; thus the reference always completes (ok == true) while the mutant can cause a revert (ok == false) for some inputs.

For any target and amount where the caller is owner and funds are available, the reference contract's sendMoney never causes the call to revert when the callee's fallback/receive reverts (it returns/continues), whereas the mutant using transfer will revert for such failing callees, so the universal rule is: calling sendMoney(owner-approved, target, amount) never reverts in the reference C for all inputs — the mutant can make it revert for some inputs.

For any target contract and any amount <= contract balance, C.sendMoney never reverts (it returns normally) even if the callee's fallback/receive reverts because C uses a low-level call and checks the boolean; the mutant using transfer will revert for a callee that reverts, so the mutant can cause sendMoney to revert for some inputs.
